Title: The Story of a New Name
The Big Sleep
Review:
I think that this novel is set in a very transitional period of detective fiction while also establishing many of the trademarks of what would become deeply ingrained in the image of a hardboiled private eye. There's this sleekness throughout the book, the dialogues are so snappy and witty, everything seems to be happening on a measured beat. I also think that this novel could have decidedly been the reason of the "heavy rain in the city" trope becoming so rooted into the noir genre.

Coming to the treatment of how women are portrayed in this book, I think that's where my opinion of The Big Sleep being a transitional novel rings the most true. The women in here are treated somewhat childishly, specially Carmen, and sometimes are used simply as a plot device but also they are strong women with a power behind their sultriness. Vivian is a miracle of writing, in how restrained her sensuality is that through the pages you can feel that teasing crawl up to you. Yes, the men talk about the women in the signature '40s way' but the women themselves are meticulously crafted and are layered where you start seeing their treatment as an admiration rather than mockery. Beyond that, the first half itself plays with a plot point that is raunchy for it's time.

There are bad things about it, certainly. There's one passage where the author censors the word fuck in the same chapter where he drops a slur. Those things, I guess, were bound to show up, but the colorful cast of characters themselves and even the fact that these archetypes are existent in this book is a surprise to me. I came out enjoying the book more than id have thought.

Title: The Silence of the Girls
Review: It is a conflicting book. Of course you cant rewrite history when you're telling a unique perspective on something that's majorly about Men in War but Brisies here is such a convoluted character. You'd think she would wish to kill everyone, but without a sign of resignation she accepts her role as the slave, You'd expect her to stand up for ANYONE, but almost every time she is a silent watcher of events, You'd expect her to hate Achilles, but she is happy to be carrying his son by the end of the book. It's a book that frames itself as voicing the unvoiced but then makes the main character a mute observer of everything. "Silence of the Girls", yeah I read the title but it wasn't a silence that was loud, just confusing. The writing itself is good, not something pristine but flows well enough to not pull you out of the story. My problems only lie with the how this book somewhat fails at doing the only thing its supposed to do.

Title: Amygdalatropolis
Review:
To me, there is a world beyond mine where exist topics which if you discuss them immediately mark you as a pervert. Even talking about those ideas to raise a point converts you into a creep who has a fascination of the taboo.

I think that is the singular reason this book shines so bright, at least for me. We want to believe in a moral binary where one side is so disgusting that we just would rather ignore its sheer existence. This little book went there, and went beyond that. It is a mirror of what growing up with internet on your fingertips feels like, and I dont think anything I have read till now comes close to Amygdalatropolis in showing how debased and virtually moral-less humans become once anonymity is provided to them. Not good, but being apathetic and selfish, rotting yet grasping for the other person's food, clapping at misery, is what being human is about, and as much as one would want to close their eyes about those aspects, it stays true for me. Rant over thanks.

Title: If on a Winter's Night a Traveler
The Plot Against America
Review:
Read in parallel with "On Zionist Literature"  by Ghassan Kanafani. 

I want to preface this by noting that the book is not at all about the struggle of Jews for their native land or about the Israel–Palestine conflict. However, because I was reading two books with very different ideologies at the same time, my experience of reading this book was heavily influenced by an ideology that vehemently denies the position taken by this book, and vice versa. 

The book is… fine. The problem is that I was expecting more, not only because this book has been hailed as one of the greatest novels of this century, but also because of the topic it tackles. On paper, it sounds like it has the opportunity to engage with a great deal. In reality, the whole story is so deeply tunnel-visioned and so afraid to make any definitive statement that one might come out more jaded than they were going in. 

I like the concept of an alternative history in which America had a Nazi-sympathizing president during World War II. What consequences could there have been? It is a frightening thought, but one has to recognize that it also is not something that happened, hence “speculative” fiction. And speculative fiction written around a great tragedy always risks turning itself into imaginary fear-mongering or a self-victimizing reality, one in which it becomes easy to ignore the privileges one group has over another simply because it is being persecuted. 

On Zionist Literature brings forward a revelation about how Jews have historically opposed assimilation and claimed exceptionality. It discusses at length how the idea of a stereotypical Jewish hero is constructed from the ground up to justify that exceptionality and to provide a rationale for the lack of interest in assimilation, or even in conversation. Herman Roth is not a Zionist in the political sense, but he does operate on a Zionist ontology. Herman Roth, the father of this family, is written in precisely that cadence of a Zionist hero. He is always skeptical of anyone who is not Jewish and consistently makes political and religious references to persecution that seems perpetually on the horizon. Roth is fully aware that many of his Jewish characters embody recognizable stereotypes: loud, argumentative, politically overinvested, anxious, omnipresent in civic life. This is not accidental, nor is it simply self-hatred. Roth has spent his entire career refusing the demand that Jewish characters be exemplary or representative. He writes Jews as messy, flawed, sometimes irritating, sometimes self-righteous, because he is resisting the idea that persecuted groups must also be morally pure. Yet by populating the novel almost exclusively with Jews who fit those profiles, Roth risks reinforcing the very images he is interrogating. His defense would be that stereotypes do not become false simply because they are stereotypes. They become dangerous when they are used as political explanations. The novel insists that even if some Jews are loud, influential, or ideologically entrenched, none of that justifies their exclusion or targeting. That is a liberal argument, not a tribal one, but it feels evasive. 

I do understand that the very topic of Jewish identity is a volatile one and that it will only become more inflamed as the conflict worsens. That said, the morality of this novel works only when considered in a vacuum. The well-adjusted American Jewish family, suddenly confronted with an unprecedented evil that may or may not happen today, tomorrow, or never, is enough to keep the caregiver constantly on edge. I can understand the over-vigilant, aggressive, and vocal response that comes from Herman. Where the problematic nature of this argument begins to show is when the family, after enduring a share of hardship, starts posing a Jew-centric morality as the correct one. The words goyim and gentile are thrown around almost as slurs, all of it occurring in front of a child who idealizes these people. I appreciate that the novel tackles ideological differences within Jewish communities, and that for the first two-thirds of the book the major conflict remains within the family itself. But what does any of this matter if, in the end, it only confirms the biases of those who refused assimilation anyway? 

The writing is strong throughout the first two acts of the book, but once past that point Roth treats the novel as though he has realized that if he pushes the analogy further, he would stand shoulder to shoulder with Zionists. The stereotypical Jew who is always roaming and destined never to find a home is present throughout the novel. Even in the end, the book affirms that perspective. Adding to this, America itself is not merely a country to Herman; it is a conditional shelter. That belief is structurally Zionist even if it rejects Israel as a solution. Zionism at its core is not about land but about the impossibility of permanent assimilation. Herman embodies that premise without embracing its institutional answer and instead places the entire burden of “taking care of the Jews” on the government. He does not ask America to protect everyone. He asks it not to betray Jews. This is understandable, but it is also ethically fraught. Roth leaves this unresolved. Why, I do not know. America under Lindbergh betrays everyone. Civil liberties erode broadly. Isolationism corrodes the moral fabric of the nation as a whole. Yet Herman cannot experience this betrayal as shared. He experiences it as confirmation. That is the crucial difference. Others feel disillusionment. He feels prophecy fulfilled. That is not moral clarity. It is narrative closure, and Roth allows us to see how comforting that closure is. 

This is where the novel is sharply not Zionist in intention but Zionist in texture. I will not even dwell on how much of a cop-out the third act is, because it ultimately says very little and collapses back into reality rather than confronting what might actually have happened and where the world could have gone. Roth seems too hesitant, too guilt-ridden, to grapple with actual persecution, spending far more time fearing it than interrogating it. 

In the end, the novel chooses psychological reassurance over ethical confrontation. It closes the circle it was best positioned to break.

Title: Ella Minnow Pea
Review: NOT a good experience. Too lost in its own gimmick, too weak to make any point against the political problems of silencing it presents. The ending is simply presented to you in a gift box tied with a sweet little bow and nobody even argues with people and their dumb interpretations of the dumb events that happen. The author was so lost in this self imposed straitjacket that he didn't even think if the world that he is building makes a singular ounce of sense. Why does the post system still exist if people have no reason to trust postmen? Why do they talk amongst themselves adhering to the same dumb imposed rules when there's like only 12 people left on the island? Why are these rules even followed as God's decree itself do they not have a braincell to tell them that putting restrictions on the kinds of sound a human voice-box can make is inherently impossible? This book is so inconsistent in it's root world-building that you cant even ask these questions without having to accept this thing as it is. Writing this review has made me angrier.

Title: The Brief History of the Dead
An Apprenticeship, or the Book of Pleasures
Review:
Translated beautifully by Stefan Tobler, flowers to him.

My experience with my first Lispector, surprisingly, was twofold, because the book itself is sitting on the two characters which are the pillars of this story. One of which is an experience that sways you in directions you weren't prepared for and the other one is written just to piss off a person like me. 

For the first, Lori is a miracle of fiminine writing. She is a girl whose life changes by going to a beach by herself and just taking a bite out of a random apple on her desk. Beyond intimacy she has put so much of her heart into her being that the "how" of being becomes almost impossible for her to decipher

I deeply DEEPLY love every part that was from Lori, and then there's the second half. Everytime I'm reminded of the fact that its ulisses who shes this obsessed with i get annoyed. He is much too persuasive and expectant of a change in her whilst Lori only feels singularly occupied by this idea of a savior-esque man who hasn't yet done anything to prove such authority.

throughout the book he promises for something of worth that lives in the future once she is deserving of it and shows not a sign of it, what it even is. all his depth and all his sadness is because of his reflection in lori.

There are many quotes from Ulisses that genuinely piss me off to an extent that It makes me wonder if Lori herself is somehow too blind to see through this guy's bullshit and if her words are somehow tricking me into believing she is more emotionally versed than she actually is. 

Conclusive thoughts? Its a beautifully written book with a core that is so deeply conservative and obsessed with traditional gender roles that reading further into it was an experience of prolonged whiplash. I see the beauty, but the form of this beauty is not according to my palate.

Title: A Short Stay in Hell
Review: Its a glorious premise wasted on this dirty excuse of a book by this incompetence manifested as an author. Throughout the book I was thinking of what could've been, and not of what I had in hand. Religion is thrown to you to make you believe that what you are getting into would deal with the constructs humans make and how things define what we are but beyond parody the religion plays no role other than for the author to talk about his ex-mormon past which he seems simply not be able to let go. Thrice in the book the author uses something akin to "I would tell you more, but I wouldn't", which maybe he hopes to convey sadness or lack of motivation for it but it comes off as a failure to tackle what topic one has picked up. The premise is beyond the author's capabilities to do justice. What he does with it is that he writes a very obvious self-insert of a character whom he can not flesh out beyond his own anecdotal flashes. Every time the story even tries to lunge for a satisfying turn the author simply quits writing more. And these are criticisms before I even arrive on how race and colour is tackled in the book. That is a tangent that deserves it's own 500 words of criticism but I wouldn't bog you down with it, rather I'd provide a quiet summary that it sounds like a liberal ex-christian's victimhood showing through pages of hell. Holy fuck I am pissed off by the existence of this book.

Title: The Safekeep
Review:
This was such a pleasant surprise, even though it won I dont know how many awards. So, so tender, so painful, and if you've ever happened to love a person for a very brief time and lost them, then probably devastating.

I am devastated, for the record. At first I had no sense of why would you set a story in 60s if you are not going to use that setting to say anything. And then, part II hits. Everything is overturn, every sincere moment of loss changes it's meaning in a very different way and you can do nothing but pulled back into that world. A world that once existed, and one which we are way better off revisiting. I have my complaints with the novel. The way the author writes dialogues is, as natural as may sound to say, is clunky and awkward in text. A very broad section of the novel was bordering on smut, every other page establishing a sort of craving, which in the larger sense of the story did matter but the amount of it was baffling to me. So, yeah, not a perfect read, but how shaken I am I think I'd remember it for a while.

Title: Dracula
Review:
Maybe the worst classic I have read, ever. Yes, It comes from a very different moment in history, yet that doesn’t place it beyond the reach of my criticism.

The book is layered with sexism and with hints of anti-immigrant hate peppered on top. It was written for the aristocrats sitting in their royal palaces to feel validated for their greatness and proud of their white heritage. The book reads like a wannabe Shakespearean play but with no emotional depth and machismic prose that serves no purpose but to solidify the disconnect of the male characters from the peasants they are so abhorred by. 

The book is written as if it is scared to cause any reaction in people. No character has any shade of personality trait. Every character of our lead bunch is a good person. Every woman in the book is prefaced with her being a "poor soul". Chapter 25 is full of discussions about "Brave men" who have given their lives and killed their own wives when time arrives to save them from the bad hands of enemy, said by a woman who has certainly done at least as much if not more than the Brave men she's glamourizing. The same woman is praised when she does something smart because she has "a man's brain". 

There's this hilarious excitement in the end where the men are so stoked to kill the vampire, comparing it with a "call to war" whereas the woman in the group is kept uninformed because she is enchanted by the vampire.

I felt like I wasted hours reading something that does not offer anything worthwhile. I don't understand how this book is considered a classic. 

(Updated the score in light of reading other vampire fiction)

Title: Gone to See the River Man
Review:
Well, what if I say I liked it? What then? 

It has become a weird pattern in past few books where I write about one thinking about another one. What Earthlings wanted to do, this book did without trying. There's always a scary side of being a human and the desperation to find a connection can lead that humanity to the edges of it where only fringes of humanity exist. Lori is in no way a protagonist, she might as well be the antagonist of this story, but you are her throughout the book. A desperate, unloved idea that wants to be written down on a paper, and doesn't care if the ink is blood. 

I hope if someone reads it, they feel the sadness of the story and not fixate on the gore of it all. It wasn't even gory, I think, everything that happened by the second half was a metaphor. Of love? Maybe. Which side, I dont know. But that is how love operates.

Play Nick Drake's River Man for the end credits of this. Let the sadness seep in.

Review:
This book is a complicated puzzle for me. 

I started the book because of no reason, having a copy on my shelf that I dragged out to fill in the gaps and thinking it'd be a quick read between my current heavy reads to fill in the gaps and as I started shifting through pages it felt barbones, passable but not extraordinary. 

I had passed through like 30% of it's length and the book has no voice of it's own, there was this certain quietness about it that echoed between the two main characters, Sofia and her mother. And I was fairly sure I wasn't having the best time of my life, but it will pass. 

And then I kept reading more, and the quiet only deepened. What you come to realize is that, this book was never meant to be loud. There are words on pages, yes, but the people talking on those pages never speak out loud. They whisper their ugliest wishes to each other, their shaking foundations which nobody ever waited for them to solidify. You learn more and more of this quiet, and the one thing this book uses so masterfully is recalling. The act of repetition, metaphorically and verbally, keeps bringing the past events back as if they are your own memory. There's a certain sardonic tone beyond the halfway point, the breaking points and the anguish, the undisclosed questions that you want answers to are not given to you. 

The four major characters for me throughout the book, Sofia, Rose, Christos and Ingrid have one thing common, and that is their detached way of showing love. There's the deepest care in each of their hearts, but they struggle to even acknowledge as if it's inhumane to feel. And that simmering volume of stress never rises above the point of boiling, because nobody is allowed to let that happen. Nobody knows that it can happen. The water would never be right. 

I found this quiet comforting, very comforting actually. The letting go comes hard, and you wouldnt know.

Title: We Do What We Do in the Dark

Review:
This book is a character assassination of Circe. If a reimagination of a character makes them stop resembling the original character then maybe as an author one has failed to do their job. 

In the greek myths Circe is one of the rare women who has always been depicted as a strong woman with a temper to be afraid of and witchery to back her infamy. She had always been interpreted as a person to be scared of, to an extent that her Sorcery was slowly modified into a sultriness by the renaissance writers making her story an allegory to the allure of beauty. That Circe, in this book, is diluted to a woman who has spent her whole life seeking validation of men surrounding her. A Circe who was feared by men that they dared not look at her direction, is raped by the first group of men she welcomes home. She has tamed lions, and wolves, and has every bit of strength to turn Aiaia upside down, and she doesn't even protest. The mischaracterisation is so appaling that it becomes borderline reductive to a character who once was mistreated but now in this book is simply "just another girl". 

Imagine being Penelope, your husband has gone away for war and you have to stay home fending off the suiters. You do that diligently. You learn of a witch who has kept your husband and made his arrival take longer than anticipated and you accept it. Your husband is back home, but with a ruined state of mind and you accept it. The witch's son arrives one day, and happens to kill your husband. You accept it. You pay the witch a visit and she ends up taking your son as her husband too? 

And I am supposed to believe that Circe was the misunderstood character all along? Every other character in the novel is more sensible and more relatable than Circe herself. How do you reimagine a character and make her worse than everyone else in a book named after her I don't understand.

Review: Boring slog, what am I doing with myself, since when did I stop having fun.

Spoiler Alerts, head on. This book lasted throughout my September and I feel like I have to write a lot just to make a mark of it's passage through these 4 weeks.


This is what I'd call a popcorn novel. In bollywood There's this concept of a masala movie which has everything, dance, drama, emotions, sex, laughs, and this book is the literary equivalent of a masala movie. The way this book is framed, structured, the "cameos", even the tantalizing premise itself is straight out of a wannabe movie and you consume it when served. That's exactly what I did. I wish to read one long novel each year, and oh how I've heard people gush about this novel so much, this one had to be this year's long novel. And it delivers, if you want to have fun and just grab your seat and shut your brain, it's so much fun. It's snappy and every event is framed so delicately that you're always looking forward for next event. King makes sure that the events, as repetitive they could get in a time-travel story, never feel so repetitive and some quirky detail flares up every time. The first half is what could basically have been a vibe check for the concept itself. 

And that's where my personal issues lie with this book. It sells you this striking premise, the cover is a newspaper cutout, the title is just a date, and NOTHING regarding that event takes place halfway through the book. The character of Al Templeton is a total mcguffin, his closeness, Jake's readiness, his obsession with the assassination, none of them are described at all. They just happen because plot needs them to happen. Jake's wife, Christy is almost a nothing character that serves the story as a ghost, a made up ghost to make you sympathize with the heroine of the novel. The book majorly takes place in the late 50s, early 60s, and there's one page, a singular semi-chapter, that discusses the racism of that era. Because again, it's a popcorn novel, it's not trying to make you think. The only second obligatory mention of a black woman happens in the final chapters as a saving grace, but that too is way too low. 

I guess that's the thing, the problem I have is that this feels manufactured. A McDonald's burger, looks good, tastes good, but you know it comes out of a factory line. Any attempt at patriotism is manufactured, any attempt at urgency is manufactured, any attempt at innovation is manufactured. The whole "what happens after you've saved kennedy" part is so, unimaginative, uncreative, an information dump that doesn't engage with itself. 

But sadly, I love McDonald's. I like the taste. I like the Sadie-George romance, as dumb and childish as it is. And fuck, I had fun. I had fun reading this. So that's where I land, glorious, switch-off-your-brain fun. Don't think about how an English Teacher is going to save America, and you'll be fine.

Title: Love Is a Dog from Hell

Review:
Theres so much about this book that annoys the hell out of me, not because it's badly written but because it tries so hard to be quirky and profound when it's clearly not. The initial chapters from the perspective of a child are written in this creepy way, which makes the main character sound too old, and when she's old, she sounds like she's still stuck in her childhood. There's no difference, in personality, worldview, or opinions during the 24 years of growing up. The characters behave like an inflated idea that only talk about what they're filled with and have no personality beyond that whatsoever. The incident of her trying to share her personal life and getting mocked for it not once but twice just felt like rubbing the point of 'Aliens dont fit on earth" onto your face, I understand that the mother is a detached person but a friend who's her age would show sympathy. These characters aren't real, they're manufactured to force a story into existence. 

The author throws "taboo" things just to entice a reaction. Sexual trauma, Incest, Cannibalism, everything that could be considered a practical taboo is in here but the author never commits to deal with either of those actions beyond their surface level inspection. Yes, the cannibalism does tie the story together in the end, but that might just be the only saving grace of this mess on paper. The book is written like a shock humor that is reactionary, asking you to wonder snarkly "You didn't think id go there did you?" while doing things more boring than being a cliche. 

Not for me. I expected better.

Helo darkness mi old frend 

So, I have to come to honesty that I had some expectations going in this book. This is the one that won Booker prize, and then the golden booker prize too. Moreover that, it was about lincoln and about grief and about loss.

I was so not prepared for how this book is written. I was so out of my mind when I first opened the pages and saw the random notes left by people of random names and nobody even knew lincoln. Review:
I was sold on the promise of this being a romance but the book was anything but.

A large breadth of this book is war, at war's worst. One could find so many parallels to the Odyssey (which the book acknowledges as well) and the perils of war, how harrowing it can be. I went through the whole book at a very sluggish pase, but there were a few scenes that stand out beyond just being about war and love. 

The fifth part of the book specially is wonderful, a quiet rumination from the perspective of everyone present during the tragedies of the first 4 chapters, I think the characters from the axis powers become real and human at this point. Also the book hits it's biggest strides here about the impotence of war, the aimlessness of the power one fights for and how the casualties of war are never the people in power. 

As I said, the sluggishness of the book was one of the biggest hurdles given that I was 100 pages deep on day 1 of reading the book. Also, there are some characters which get lost in the noise of war, particularly Ella which could have had so much to offer, but that perspective is lost in exchange of the descriptions of torture. The yearning, did not work for me, but these days barely any emotion does. It is one of the better reads of this year for me though.

Title: Sphere
Review:
I wanted to have a McDonald's burger and what I got was a quick meal I cant complain about but god was this a big racist misogynist burger that I just gobbled down. 

Good things about it? The pacing is fantastic, and thats it. Had this 500 page book been paced in any other way thats not the way it's paced here this would've been the death of me and maybe would've ended my will to read anymore but even I am surprised how quickly these 500 pages passed. That alone was something that made this book bearable and raised its enjoyment. 

The bad? Everything else. Genuinely everything else theres not a single saving grace for this book beyond the somewhat interesting plot in the first half and how quickly it ends. 

I am a big proponent of authorial intent and i like to believe that the author is not retarded but aware of what they are writing and the writing should be looked from the framework where you acknowledge the author to be smart enough, given all that Crichton surely had set out to write a bunch of deeply racist characters and a caricature of black man for his sci fi odyssey I guess.

He writes harry as a scrawny mathematics prodigy and then pokes jungian psychology just enough to imply that the psychosexual things going on with harrys characterization is because he was never good with sports and wasnt muscular and strong hence his "shadow self" needs expression via these violent actions which are also somehow childish. He does the exact same thing writing Beth as this person who is very physically active and strong, and then frames this as some sort of inversion of what the narrator's idea of a woman should be. As our great psychologist narrator frames, beth wants to be strong and outspoken because she deeply feels bad about not being the soft spoken tiny little women she should be. Like, What the fuck are you writing about Crichton?

The book is driven by this white-man's-perspective where every black man is an intellectual and sexual threat and every woman is a punching bag to excercise your manlihood on by demeaning her, telling her she's intellectually impotent and then by the end of the book making her an object of sex itself. And that all is just problems with the books characterization of the people, there's writing too, writing that is godawful. 

Every concept introduced is explained to you like youre a newborn and the people talking aren't supposed to be phd holders. Exposition is the only way the author knows to talk about things, and had Wikipedia existed back when the book was written the author would've soiled his pants out of sheer joy. The writing is so self-focused that if a character is not the main one narrating the events, they simply dont matter in the broader sense. What a shame that the characters that are not the narrator are...a woman and a black man, to Suffer the wrath of a mediocre fetishist who presents his bullshit ideas wrapped in the wrapper of psychology. 

The book does show remarkable variety in the ways it can be racist though, and it makes you wonder if some of the authors real life experiences with racism and sexism would make him tackle these themes with such nuance but hey that is something not for me to judge. 

Verdict : Dogshit. Don't read if youre easily swayed by racist or misogynist  ideas because you'll think it's great sci fi writing, its not.
